JevOut: Natural Context Can Flip Decision Models

Abstract

An ordinary-looking background detail can turn a correct model decision into a confident mistake. We demonstrate this fragility in four decision systems, including Jev, across seven datasets covering knowledge, reasoning, and tool routing. Within 64 accepted target evaluations per decision, we uncover short context additions that redirect 61.4%–73.2% of each system’s initially correct decisions toward a wrong option fixed in advance. The additions supply background or procedural information rather than explicit answer-selection instructions, leaving the original question and choices intact. We construct them through probability-guided context optimization, which uses shifts in the option distribution to refine surrounding text under naturalness and answer-preservation constraints. Redirection affects initially confident decisions, often produces high-confidence wrong choices, and transfers across models. In blinded human evaluation, 91.6% of 250 sampled successful contexts are judged natural, answer-preserving, and free of decisive answer-changing evidence by a majority of three independent annotators. These findings expose a weakness in current decision models: context that looks entirely compatible with an input can redirect the choices that agents, routers, and evaluators rely on.

Homepage: https://xzx34.github.io/jevout/
Code: https://github.com/xzx34/JevOut

1 Introduction

Language-model systems increasingly turn open-ended language into bounded choices that drive downstream behavior. An agent selects a tool or its next action, a router directs a request, and a model-based evaluator chooses among candidate responses (Schick et al., 2023; Yao et al., 2023; Zheng et al., 2023; Patil et al., 2025). We study decision models that expose this step as a probability distribution over a specified set of options. This interface allows downstream software to use model probabilities directly, without first interpreting a free-form response. These decisions are made in context: inputs can include conversation history, background details, retrieved evidence, or descriptions of the surrounding state.

A detail can fit naturally with an input without changing which option is correct. We find that short additions of this kind can nevertheless redirect an initially correct decision toward a wrong option fixed in advance. We call this phenomenon natural-context redirection. Rather than instructing the model to select an answer, the addition supplies background or procedural detail relevant to the original input. The question and available choices stay unchanged, yet the selected option and its probability can shift sharply. Figure 1 illustrates this behavior on a climate-ethics question: an added sentence about intergenerational consequences redirects the decision without changing the definition being asked for.

Prior work shows that language models are sensitive to prompt formatting, demonstration order, option order, and the placement of relevant evidence (Ishibashi et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2022; Pezeshkpour and Hruschka, 2024; Liu et al., 2024). Fluent, answer-preserving additions can also mislead question-answering models, while model-based evaluators exhibit systematic sensitivity to controlled changes in their inputs (Cao et al., 2022; Ye et al., 2025). Our focus is how this sensitivity carries over to finite-choice decision interfaces, where both the selected option and its probability can affect downstream behavior. We study whether naturally fitting additions can redirect a correct choice toward a fixed wrong option, and use the full option distribution to measure and uncover that redirection.

For each target model, we retain the items it initially answers correctly and fix one incorrect option per item as the target. We construct answer-preserving context additions: the original source, question, and choices stay fixed, and additions must fit naturally while preserving the correct answer. Probability-guided context optimization uses the full option distribution to guide this construction. Even before the selected option changes, a candidate can increase the target’s probability relative to its strongest competitor. We use this graded signal to prioritize candidates for further refinement under the same semantic constraints. A targeted flip occurs when the model selects the fixed wrong target. Targeted Flip Rate (TFR) measures the proportion of initially correct decisions for which we uncover at least one such flip within a fixed budget of accepted target evaluations.

We evaluate four decision systems—Jev, OpenSourceJev, Von, and a plain Qwen scorer—across seven datasets covering knowledge, reasoning, and tool routing. Within 64 accepted target evaluations per decision, context optimization uncovers targeted flips in 61.4%–73.2% of each system’s initially correct decisions. Redirection occurs in every model–dataset combination, including next-tool choices in recorded dialogues. The effect reaches originally confident decisions, and many successful contexts contain only a single added sentence. In a blinded evaluation with three independent annotators, 91.6% of 250 successful contexts sampled across systems meet all three validity criteria by majority judgment: naturalness, answer preservation, and absence of decisive answer-changing evidence.

Frozen contexts also redirect other systems without further optimization. Probability feedback helps uncover these contexts: on 140 matched initially correct Jev decisions, probability-based allocation improves TFR over label-based allocation at the same evaluation budget. Training the proposer on development trajectories for the same target also improves direct context generation on held-out items without intermediate target feedback. Together, these results identify a weakness in using decision models as interfaces between language and action: ordinary-looking context can alter the choice they recommend even when the appropriate answer stays the same.

2 Related Work

Behavioral testing evaluates models against expectations about how their predictions should respond to controlled input changes. CheckList includes invariance tests for changes that should leave a prediction unchanged (Ribeiro et al., 2020). Adversarial reading comprehension gives a concrete instance of this concern: Jia and Liang (2017) add distracting sentences to passages without changing their correct answers, yet substantially degrade model performance. TASA combines edits to the answer-bearing sentence with a fluent distracting sentence while preserving the gold answer (Cao et al., 2022). These studies show that preserving the correct answer does not ensure a stable model prediction. We examine the same tension in finite-choice decision models, keeping the original source and option schema intact while adding naturally fitting context. We measure redirection from a correct decision to one wrong option fixed before construction, along with the probability assigned to that option.

Model-based evaluation studies a related reliability problem when model judgments determine rankings, preferences, or scores (Zheng et al., 2023). Controlled studies find sensitivity to response position and other features beyond the quality being assessed (Ye et al., 2025; Shi et al., 2025). Raina et al. (2024) optimize universal phrases that alter assessments and transfer across evaluators, with stronger effects on absolute scoring than on comparative assessment. Our contexts are instead constructed for individual decision items and must preserve their correct answers. We focus on redirecting a choice with a known correct answer, rather than changing how a candidate response is assessed. The construction process also connects to automatic prompt optimization, which uses evaluated proposals or textual feedback to refine language inputs (Pryzant et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2024). Here, the refinement signal is the target’s probability relative to its strongest competitor, and the editable text is the surrounding context rather than the task instruction. Appendix A covers learned context generation and concurrent decision-model studies.

3 Natural-Context Redirection

3.1 Setting and Context Additions

We study language-based decision models that return probabilities over a finite set of options. A decision u=(x,q,C,y)u=(x,q,C,y) consists of source context xx, question qq, options CC, and correct option yy. The model assigns probabilities pθ​(c∣x,q,C)p_{\theta}(c\mid x,q,C) and returns a selected option y^θ\widehat{y}_{\theta}. We retain the population UθU_{\theta} whose original selection is correct and fix the most probable wrong option as the target: tu=arg​maxc∈C∖{y}⁡pθ​(c∣x,q,C)t_{u}=\argmax_{c\in C\setminus\{y\}}p_{\theta}(c\mid x,q,C). The target remains fixed throughout construction. Multi-answer tasks use binary option-membership decisions, retaining one eligible absent option per source item (Appendix B.2).

An answer-preserving context addition supplies background or procedural detail that fits the input without changing its correct answer. A context z=((b1,a1),…,(bL,aL))z=((b_{1},a_{1}),\ldots,(b_{L},a_{L})) specifies added sentences ala_{l} and insertion boundaries blb_{l}. Its rendering xz=ℛ⁡(x,z)x_{z}=\mathcal{R}(x,z) preserves every original character in order, with the question, options, and their order unchanged. Structural preservation is enforced during rendering. The semantic feasible set 𝒵u\mathcal{Z}_{u} requires natural fit, answerability, the same complete correct-answer set, and no explicit answer-selection cues. An addition can introduce a relevant fact or shift emphasis, provided that it neither makes a different answer correct nor makes the original answer ambiguous.

A targeted flip occurs only when the augmented input selects tut_{u}. Write Iu(z)=𝟙[y^θ(xz,q,C)=tu]I_{u}(z)=\mathds{1}[\widehat{y}_{\theta}(x_{z},q,C)=t_{u}] and let ℰB​(u)\mathcal{E}_{B}(u) contain accepted contexts evaluated within BB target calls. Targeted Flip Rate counts decisions with at least one such flip:

TFR⁡(B)=1|Uθ|​∑u∈Uθmaxz∈ℰB​(u)⁡Iu​(z).\operatorname{TFR}(B)=\frac{1}{|U_{\theta}|}\sum_{u\in U_{\theta}}\max_{z\in\mathcal{E}_{B}(u)}I_{u}(z). (1)

The maximum is zero when no context is evaluated. A change to another wrong option does not count; rejections and unsuccessful runs retain their place in the original denominator. Appendix B.1 defines probability thresholds and matching rules.

3.2 Probability-Guided Context Optimization

The option distribution reveals progress before the selected decision changes. Increasing the target probability alone need not make it the preferred option: a competing option may still receive more mass. We therefore maximize the log-probability margin between the target and its strongest competitor over feasible contexts:

maxz∈𝒵u⁡mu​(z),mu​(z)=log⁡pθ​(tu∣xz,q,C)+ϵmaxc≠tu⁡pθ​(c∣xz,q,C)+ϵ.\begin{gathered}\max_{z\in\mathcal{Z}_{u}}m_{u}(z),\\ m_{u}(z)=\log\frac{p_{\theta}(t_{u}\mid x_{z},q,C)+\epsilon}{\max_{c\neq t_{u}}p_{\theta}(c\mid x_{z},q,C)+\epsilon}.\end{gathered} (2)

Here ϵ>0\epsilon>0 keeps the margin finite. A positive margin makes the target the unique most probable option. The margin guides construction; the model’s returned selection determines whether a targeted flip occurred.

A language-model proposer, conditioned on the original item, gold answer, fixed target, and current context, generates one sentence and insertion boundary. Mechanical checks enforce placement and remove duplicates or explicit selection text. A separate invocation of the base model evaluates the completed context for natural fit and answer preservation, without seeing the wrong target or optimization score. This automatic check implements the semantic acceptance rule (Appendix C). Each accepted context receives a target evaluation and enters an archive 𝒜r\mathcal{A}_{r} together with its option distribution; the original input is also retained.

The archive allows later proposals to extend contexts that have already moved probability toward the target. To allocate a finite set of refinements, we balance the expected margin of selected parents against the entropy of their allocation. Let Δr\Delta_{r} be the probability simplex over 𝒜r\mathcal{A}_{r} and H(v)=−∑jvjlogvjH(v)=-\sum_{j}v_{j}\log v_{j}. The allocation objective is

g(r)=arg​maxv∈Δr⁡{∑jvj​mu​(zj)+TH⁡(v)}.g^{(r)}=\argmax_{v\in\Delta_{r}}\left\{\sum_{j}v_{j}m_{u}(z_{j})+TH(v)\right\}. (3)

Its solution assigns weight proportional to exp⁡(mu​(zj)/T)\exp(m_{u}(z_{j})/T). We mix this distribution with uniform allocation:

πj(r)=(1−η)​gj(r)+η|𝒜r|.\pi_{j}^{(r)}=(1-\eta)g_{j}^{(r)}+\frac{\eta}{|\mathcal{A}_{r}|}. (4)

Temperature T>0T>0 controls concentration on larger margins, while η∈(0,1)\eta\in(0,1) gives every recorded context a positive allocation probability. The resulting allocation favors contexts with larger target margins while retaining exploration; Appendix D.2 derives the rule.

Each iteration extends sampled parents and archives their evaluated children for the next iteration. Original-input restarts explore new additions alongside refinements of previous contexts. We use 16 proposal slots for up to four iterations, reserving four slots for original-input restarts after the first iteration. Each rejected proposal gets one retry and uses no target call. Construction stops after a completed iteration reaches a targeted flip with probability at least 0.7, or at the iteration limit, giving at most 64 accepted target evaluations. Appendix D provides pseudocode, the allocation derivation, and complete execution settings.

3.3 Learning to Generate Contexts

Optimization trajectories also provide supervision for proposing contexts on new items. Each trajectory records an original decision, its fixed target, the generated additions, and their resulting margins. These records support two forms of supervision: predicting a useful next addition from an existing context, or predicting a complete successful context from the original item.

We adapt the same base proposer with LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) while fixing the target model and checker. V1 learns next-addition transitions, weighting examples within each item by their resulting margin. V2 learns complete successful contexts with item-balanced supervision before length filtering. Both use the same backbone, adapter configuration, and optimizer. At evaluation, a common complete-context prompt tests direct generation on held-out items without intermediate target feedback. Appendix H gives the loss, corpus construction, length filtering, and training schedules.

4 Experiments

4.1 Experimental Setup

Tasks and populations. We evaluate knowledge questions (MMLU-Pro and SuperGPQA), narrative and social reasoning (MuSR and ToMBench), legal reasoning (LAR-ECHR), multi-answer selection (SATA-Bench), and tool routing (BFCL V4) (Wang et al., 2024; M-A-P Team et al., 2025; Sprague et al., 2024; Chen et al., 2024; Chlapanis et al., 2024; Xu et al., 2025a; Patil et al., 2025). These tasks expose different places for surrounding context: before a standalone question, within a passage, or inside the final user message of a tool-routing checkpoint. Each dataset contributes 50 development and 100 held-out source items. Development items support method development and proposer training; the resulting 700-item test set is item-disjoint. For each target, we retain at most one initially correct decision unit per source item, including for the binary reduction of SATA. Appendix B.2 specifies the adaptations, source splits, and target-specific populations.

Models. The targets comprise hosted Jev 1.13.0 (TypeSafe AI, 2025), the open Jev-style implementation OpenSourceJev (OpenSourceJev Contributors, 2026), Von 1.0, and a plain Qwen scorer. OpenSourceJev and the plain scorer share frozen Qwen3-1.7B Q8 weights (Qwen Team, 2025) but use different interfaces: the former scores typed branches, while the latter directly scores numbered options. Von is a 395M non-autoregressive decision model (Von Contributors, 2026). Gemma4-12B proposes additions, and a separate invocation checks their constraints without seeing the target option (Gemma Team, 2026). Scoring interfaces and prompts are specified in Appendices B.3 and C.

Controls and budget. Neutral one-shot generates one sentence without seeing the target option; target-aware one-shot receives it. Both use the optimizer’s base proposer and acceptance checks. Context optimization allows up to 64 accepted target evaluations per decision, excluding the initial eligibility evaluation. We also compare repeated independent target-aware generation under the same ceiling of accepted target calls on Jev. All rates retain the initially correct population, including decisions for which no accepted context succeeds; intervals are 95% Wilson intervals unless stated otherwise. The primary runs span 1,449 eligible model–item pairs. Appendix D.4 gives the complete protocol, and Appendix I.1 records proposal counts, accepted calls, and stopping outcomes.

4.2 Redirection across Models and Tasks

Natural-context redirection occurs across all four decision systems. Under the fixed evaluation budget, TFR ranges from 61.4% to 73.2% on their respective initially correct populations in Table 1. Many of the resulting wrong choices also receive high probability. For each system, a majority of its successful cases include a context that assigns at least 0.7 probability to the fixed target. The added detail can thus make the wrong option dominate the output distribution, rather than merely change the winner of a near-tie.

The task breakdown in Figure 2 reveals variation within this broad pattern. All model–task combinations admit targeted flips, spanning question-only, passage, and dialogue inputs. Legal reasoning has the lowest observed TFR for Jev and OpenSourceJev, whereas tool routing has the highest for both. On the tool-routing items, the addition changes neither the earlier dialogue nor the available function schemas; it enters only the final user message. The resulting redirection changes which tool the model selects next. The same phenomenon seen in answer selection therefore also reaches a decision that specifies the next software action.

Human validation. Independent judgments support the semantic validity of most sampled redirections. Three independent annotators assessed 250 successful contexts sampled across the four systems, mixed with 100 accepted-but-unsuccessful controls and blinded to the target, prediction, and outcome. By majority judgment, 91.6% of successes were natural, preserved the gold answer, and introduced no decisive answer-changing evidence. The controls had a similar validity rate of 93.0%. Appendix C.1 details sampling, judgment criteria, and agreement.

4.3 Confident Decisions and Short Contexts

High initial confidence does not prevent redirection. Within Jev, the most confident group in Figure 3a is less susceptible than the lower-confidence groups, but still contains many redirected decisions. Each system’s highest-confidence stratum admits targeted flips in Table 2. In each system, contexts can move probability from a strongly favored correct option to the fixed wrong alternative, often making that alternative highly probable as well. Redirection is therefore not confined to initially uncertain decisions.

The two probability thresholds refer to the same decision before and after context is added. Within each system, they identify cases that begin with a concentrated distribution on the correct option and end with a concentrated distribution on the wrong target. This matters for applications that consume probabilities alongside the selected label: the context can change both the choice and the apparent strength of support for it. Appendix F gives the complete strata and confidence intervals.

Much of the observed redirection can be achieved with little added text. A single added sentence suffices for 41.5% of the original initially correct Jev population. Restricting the recorded successful contexts by word count in Figure 3b measures how much coverage short additions retain. The 64-word cap retains most decisions redirected by the full procedure, a pattern also present in the other systems in Table 3. Even the stricter 32-word cap covers a sizable part of each eligible population. The model can thus favor a wrong alternative even when a compact addition leaves the original evidence and choices intact.

4.4 Probability Feedback and Evaluation Budget

Redirections appear early in optimization, and additional evaluations continue to uncover new cases. Across all four systems in Figure 4a, most of the final successes are already found within the first 16 accepted calls. The curves continue upward through the full budget, with diminishing gains.

Target information already helps at the first proposal: target-aware one-shot outperforms neutral generation on every system in Table 1. Repeated independent generation uncovers many more flips, reaching 48.0% TFR on the same 508 Jev decisions under the optimizer’s 64-call ceiling. Full context optimization adds a further 13.4 percentage points. The two procedures find nearly the same number of flips at the first 16-call prefix; their coverage separates as more evaluations become available. Independent proposals discover much of the phenomenon, while the complete refinement procedure extends coverage beyond this control. Appendix J reports the paired outcomes and budget curves.

Probability feedback helps decide which contexts merit further refinement. We compare probability-only and label-only allocation on 140 matched initially correct Jev decisions, with numerical history hidden from the proposer in both conditions. The former weights parents by target margin; the latter uses a binary indicator of target selection. Until a flip occurs, that binary score gives the same value to every archived context, whereas the margin distinguishes candidates closer to selecting the target.

At 64 accepted evaluations, probability-based allocation improves TFR by 7.1 percentage points over label-based allocation. The paired differences in Figure 4b increase with the evaluation budget; at 64 calls, the 95% interval excludes zero. Here the probabilities help through parent selection: the proposer receives no numerical history in either condition. Full feedback, which also exposes that history to the proposer, does not exceed the observed probability-only rate. The full paired analysis is in Appendix G.1.

4.5 Cross-Model Transfer

Contexts constructed for one model can redirect another toward the same wrong option without further optimization. We evaluate each frozen context on destinations that initially answer the exact source-selected unit correctly, retaining the source’s fixed target. The matched populations include source failures as well as successes. Every directed pair in Figure 5 exhibits targeted transfer, so the effect is not confined to the model that supplied the construction feedback.

Transfer is strongest in both directions between OpenSourceJev and plain Qwen. Their shared weights permit us to evaluate the same contexts through different scoring interfaces; changing the interface leaves many of these redirections intact. Transfer also occurs outside this shared-backbone pair, where rates range from 21.1% to 31.2% across the matched populations.

4.6 Learning from Optimization Trajectories

Optimization trajectories provide supervision that improves context generation on new items. We evaluate the transition-trained V1 and context-trained V2 alongside Base on the same 508 initially correct Jev decisions. All use a common complete-context prompt that produces one to four additions without intermediate target feedback. Both trained proposers achieve higher one-generation TFR than Base in Table 4. For V2, the gain is 5.7 percentage points. The evaluation items are held out from training, so successful development contexts provide useful supervision for new decision problems.

The improvement persists when each proposer is allowed four independent generations and target evaluations select the accepted context with the highest margin. Both trained models remain above Base under this best-of-four comparison. Training and generating more candidates thus provide complementary ways to uncover redirections: the trained proposers improve the first generation, and selection among several generations adds coverage for each. Appendix H gives the training recipes, task-level results, and paired tests.

5 Conclusion

Natural-context redirection exposes a weakness in how decision models use surrounding information. Across four systems and seven datasets, short additions can redirect an initially correct decision to a fixed wrong option while preserving the underlying task and answer. This behavior reaches originally confident choices and can persist when a context is transferred to another model. Probability-guided context optimization makes these failures observable by refining additions that shift the option distribution.

Bounded decisions connect language to software actions. Our results show that their reported probabilities can shift with details that leave the appropriate choice unchanged. Evaluating these interfaces therefore requires examining how surrounding context affects both the selected option and its probability. A dependable decision model must distinguish context that changes the correct choice from context that merely changes which option it favors.

Limitations

The evaluation covers English tasks with finite option sets and known correct answers. These tasks make it possible to distinguish contextual redirection from a legitimate change in the answer. Extending this analysis to multilingual inputs, open-ended actions, or decisions without an agreed reference answer requires corresponding criteria for answer preservation.

We evaluate individual decisions, including next-tool choices within recorded dialogues. In an interactive system, a redirected action can change subsequent observations and decisions. Measuring how redirection propagates through such sequences requires evaluation in a closed-loop environment. The present decision-level results identify a source of fragility at the interface through which those systems select their actions.

Ethical Considerations

The evaluation uses public benchmark tasks and bounded choices to study decision reliability. Contexts that redirect routing or tool selection have dual-use implications when transferred to operational systems. The intended use is to identify and measure these failure modes before models control downstream actions. Testing operational systems should be conducted with authorization and safeguards against unintended actions.
